title: Hydrogen-terminated diamond access channel using surface transfer doping
idea: Effect: surface transfer doping. A bonded thin diamond film with an H-terminated surface and MoO3 acceptor cap forms a 2D hole gas that the wordline depletes; the 5.5 eV bulk band gap makes thermal generation essentially nil, and diamond's ~2000 W/mK conductivity spreads array heat.
why: Leakage tail and thermal (fact 3): retention hours and no high-temperature refresh doubling; bonded diamond layers are a route to cool 3D tiers (fact 2).

title: KV-cache significance split: mantissa tails in unrefreshed rows
idea: LLM KV caches tolerate noise in low-order mantissa bits. Keep sign, exponent and top mantissa bits in normally refreshed ECC rows, and put the low 4-5 mantissa bits of each BF16/FP8 value in rows refreshed only at their 1%-BER age with no ECC, so softmax sees those flips as tiny noise.
why: Facts 3 and 5: ~30-40% of KV bits drop most refresh and all parity, cutting HBM refresh energy and ECC overhead; expected perplexity change <0.1%.

title: Bubble-wrap void beneath each storage-node junction
idea: Random stimulus 'bubble wrap': air pockets isolate whatever sits on top. Form a silicon-on-nothing cavity (Si/SiGe epi, SiGe removed laterally, top Si sealed by H2 anneal) under the storage-node junction only, so the junction has no bottom area facing the substrate while the channel stays body-tied.
why: Removes bottom-area junction generation leakage and substrate-injected minority carriers (fact 3), aiming at 5-10x lower junction leakage without floating-body effects in the channel.

title: Substitute helium backside cooling with hydrogen for cryogenic implants
idea: Substitute the helium backside gas in the implanter chuck with low-pressure H2, which conducts heat even better than helium, to hold wafers at -100 C during storage-node junction implants. The cold implant fully amorphizes the region, which then regrows by solid-phase epitaxy without end-of-range dislocation loops.
why: End-of-range defects sit inside the storage-junction depletion region and drive SRH junction leakage; removing them cuts tail leakage ~3-10x.

title: One global clock restores every cell: gated-diode charge-pump bistables
idea: Inverts 'refresh is done row by row by sense amps': each cell is a gated diode (large capacitance when inverted, small when depleted) tied to a shared plate clock and a diode to the supply; a stored '1' couples the clock strongly and is topped up each cycle while a '0' couples weakly and stays below the diode threshold, so one global clock refreshes billions of cells at once.
why: Lets cheap leaky TFT or poly cells work with no row refresh, sense-amp refresh path or refresh controller (fact 7), ~2 devices per cell in low-mask tiers, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: continuous clock power and margin between stable points.

title: Thermally drawn multimaterial fibers as one-dimensional memory substrates
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: replace the 2D wafer with a 1D substrate. A macroscopic preform of chalcogenide-glass semiconductor, polymer dielectric and metal electrodes is thermally drawn into kilometres of fiber whose cross-section is one memory column (bitline, storage electrodes, access channel); fibers are then woven or laminated with orthogonal wordline fibers into 3D blocks.
why: Capital intensity (Fact 4): draw towers make kilometres per hour with no lithography, and wide-gap chalcogenides give low leakage (Fact 3); density and speed are highly speculative.

title: Z-channel asymmetric codes match one-directional decay errors
idea: Physics says retention errors go only one way: charged cells lose charge and never gain it. After true/anti-cell mapping, every decay error is therefore a charged-to-empty flip. Implement an asymmetric (Z-channel) error-correcting code, such as Varshamov-Tenengolts or a constant-weight-augmented BCH, in an FPGA controller; it needs about half the parity of a symmetric code. Extend refresh until the decay BER reaches the code's budget. Fits $1M and 24 months.
why: Running at 4-8x longer refresh with ~3-6% parity overhead cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss in proportion (fact 3).

title: Floating negative wordlines replace standby charge pumps
idea: In self-refresh, a single capacitive kick (domino-precharge style) drives all idle wordlines to about -0.6 V, after which they float and their own capacitance holds the bias, topped up rarely by a tiny timer.
why: Keeps the 10-100x leakage benefit of a negative wordline without the static power of an always-on negative pump, cutting standby current 20-30%.

title: Erasable conductive ferroelectric domain walls as nondestructive bits
idea: Po: the wire appears and disappears. In a thin-film lithium niobate cell, a pulse between two side electrodes nucleates a charged domain wall that conducts ~1e4x better than the bulk, and an opposite pulse erases it; reading wall current is nondestructive, so the bit needs neither capacitor nor refresh.
why: Facts 1, 3 and 8: no capacitor, refresh or restore, with ns domain switching; risk is LiNbO3-on-Si integration and wall current at 20 nm.

title: Substitute plasma channel thinning with thermal atomic-layer etching
idea: Substitute argon-ion or plasma recess of ultrathin channels with thermal atomic-layer etching (oxidation/fluorination plus ligand-exchange cycles, N2 purged). It removes ~0.1 nm per cycle with no ion damage and sets channel body thickness to within one monolayer.
why: Body-thickness variation is a leading source of Vt scatter in thin channels; monolayer control halves sigma-Vt and shrinks the leakage tail ~10x.

title: Electric eel's stacked cells: voltage-stacked subarrays reuse one charge
idea: An electric eel stacks thousands of low-voltage cells in series. Four subarrays sit in a series voltage stack across a 2.2 V rail, each in its own 0.55 V domain, so charge one subarray draws while sensing flows on as the next one's supply; a small push-pull regulator balances mismatched activity.
why: Each supply coulomb is used four times (~4x) and the low per-domain swing cuts CV^2 (~2.5x), together ~10x lower energy per access from the rail, with less current delivery and IR loss.

title: EV-battery second life: retention-graded DRAM cascade with refresh tags
idea: Adapted from the second-life market for retired EV batteries: the module SPD gains fields for a measured retention class and required refresh multiplier; retired server modules are re-profiled and resold into edge, PC or cache roles where 2x refresh or lower operating temperature is acceptable.
why: Raises usable supply without new wafers: modules with drifted leakage tails (fact 3) get a second service life instead of shredding, and the tags let controllers run them safely.

title: Aviation line-replaceable units: swappable refresh-and-periphery die
idea: Adapted from aircraft line-replaceable units, built to be swapped on the flight line: split each DRAM into an array die (cells, access devices, sense amps) and a separately mounted periphery die carrying refresh scheduling, temperature sensing, ECC and retention maps, joined by a reworkable fine-pitch interposer, so the refresh brain is upgraded or replaced without discarding the array.
why: Arrays outlive their refresh logic; a replaceable refresh engine lets old arrays gain new retention-aware algorithms (fact 3) and moves part of the 49% periphery area (fact 7) onto a cheaper node.

title: Eliminate inter-cell dielectric: air-gap isolation against passing-gate leakage
idea: Replace STI oxide between adjacent cells with sealed air-gap trenches (sacrificial poly removed by XeF2, sealed by PECVD), so passing wordlines couple far less into neighbouring storage nodes and no trapped oxide charge sits at the isolation edge.
why: Passing-gate effects and STI-edge traps feed the retention tail and row hammer (facts 3, 9); k=1 vs 3.9 cuts coupling ~4x using standard university MEMS steps.

title: Substitute oxide isolation with sacrificial-carbon air gaps near passing gates
idea: Substitute the dielectric between passing (neighbor) wordlines and the storage-node junction with an air gap: amorphous carbon is deposited from C2H2/H2 with no argon or helium dilution, then burned out through a porous cap in O2.
why: Passing-gate coupling modulates storage-junction leakage whenever neighbors switch; an air gap (k ~1) cuts that coupling ~3x, reducing activity-dependent leakage and row-hammer-like retention loss.

title: Eliminate dopants: polarization-induced 2DEG GaN access transistor
idea: Replace the doped Si access device with an AlGaN/GaN heterostructure whose channel electrons come from spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization rather than dopants, turned off with a recessed p-GaN gate. No implant, no random dopant fluctuation and a 3.4 eV gap remove the junction and thermal-generation leakage tail.
why: Intrinsic carrier density ~1e-10 cm^-3 vs 1e10 in Si; leakage could fall >1000x, pushing retention to seconds and removing most refresh energy; GaN-on-Si is an existing U.S. power-electronics process. Array-density integration is unproven.

title: Ruthenium buried-wordline gate replaces tungsten and channel doping
idea: Worse: use tungsten wordlines (China ~80%) with heavy channel doping to set Vt, adding random-dopant leakage tails. Flip: use a high-work-function Ru buried gate (~4.8 eV, electromigration-robust at 125 C) to set Vt with a near-undoped channel, removing random-dopant fluctuation.
why: Tightens the leakage tail (fact 3), removes a tungsten chokepoint, and stays stable over a 10-year 125 C life.

title: Second life for leaky silicon: refresh-tuned salvage of retention rejects
idea: Inverts 'a die that fails 64 ms retention is scrap': buy fab retention-reject dies and decommissioned server and phone DRAM at scrap prices, profile each chip's retention map on high-throughput testers, and mount them on CXL boards whose controller refreshes at the measured interval (4-8 ms) and remaps the worst rows.
why: Marginal cost is scrap value plus test (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x cheaper per GB, adding supply with no fab and U.S.-sited refurbishment; trade-off is higher refresh energy, ~10-20% bandwidth loss and heterogeneous parts.

title: Read-restoring gain cell where every read tops up storage node
idea: Po: reading is refreshing. In a 2T capacitorless gain cell, add a diode-connected feedback from the read path so read current through a 1 cell briefly pulls its storage gate back toward full level, while a 0 cell draws no current and stays low; any row read regularly never needs a separate refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 8: hot rows refresh themselves for free and reads stay nondestructive; with typical access patterns 50%+ of refreshes vanish.

title: Bank-wide ferroelectric back gate flips array Vt for sleep
idea: Effect: remanent ferroelectric polarization. A shared HZO back gate under each subarray's vertical-channel transistors is pulsed once on self-refresh entry to polarization 'down', adding ~0.4 V of nonvolatile back-bias that shuts the leakage tail with no continuous negative pump; on exit a pulse restores 'up' for full drive.
why: Idle refresh power (fact 3): self-refresh interval x10-30 with zero standby bias power; removes negative-bias pump area from periphery (fact 7).

title: Zone-refined access pillars sweep deep-trap metals into a sacrificial cap
idea: Borrow ingot zone refining: scan a nanosecond-laser molten zone up each vertical access-transistor pillar topped with a sacrificial a-Si cap, so Fe/Cu/Ni deep-level impurities (segregation coefficient k<<1) ride the melt front into the cap, which CMP then removes.
why: Fact 3: the <=13 fA tail is set by rare cells hosting SRH deep traps; purging them could cut tail cells ~10x, pushing worst-case retention toward 0.5-1 s and cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss by up to ~80%.

title: Ephemeral-grade DRAM: sell retention rejects to frame-buffer users
idea: Camera, display and network ring buffers overwrite every byte within ~16 ms. Create a product grade for dies that fail the 64 ms retention screen but pass at 16-32 ms, sold to customers whose controllers guarantee a rewrite cadence and issue no refresh at all.
why: Scarce supply: turns retention-fail scrap and downbins (a few % of output) into usable bits, and these buyers spend zero refresh energy; adds supply without a new fab.

title: CoZrTa magnetic inductors make refresh adiabatic, recycling bitline charge
idea: Co: integrate thin-film amorphous CoZrTa inductors in the DRAM BEOL, one per bank, so restore swings during refresh are driven as resonant LC ramps instead of abrupt switching, and charge from discharging bitlines is returned to the tank for the next row.
why: Refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, fact 3) is mostly bitline CV^2; resonant/adiabatic restore can recover ~50-70%, roughly halving refresh energy.

title: Lattice-matched GaP pocket on the storage side kills band-to-band tunnelling
idea: TRIZ #4 Asymmetry: the access transistor needs a high bandgap only where it leaks, not where it drives. Selectively grow a lattice-matched GaP pocket (Eg 2.26 eV, ~0.4% mismatch to Si) on just the storage-node side of the recessed channel; band-to-band tunnelling falls roughly exponentially with Eg^1.5 while the Si bitline side keeps full drive.
why: GIDL under negative wordline bias is a dominant tail mechanism (Fact 3): claim ~100x lower GIDL, allowing a shallower negative wordline (smaller pumps, Fact 10) and 4-8x longer refresh.

title: Milk-carton expiry dates let dying data skip refresh
idea: Random stimulus 'milk carton expiry date': some contents are gone before they spoil. The compiler/runtime tags allocations (activations, KV-cache tiles, gradient buffers) with a deadline; a per-row expiry register in the DRAM refresh engine skips refresh for any row whose data is guaranteed overwritten or freed before its retention window ends.
why: In AI training most HBM rows are rewritten within 10-60 ms; skipping them cuts refresh operations 50-80% and recovers much of the 10-20% bandwidth tax (fact 3).

title: Drip-irrigation farmer: 0.5 fF planar cells with virtual-ground sensing
idea: Drip irrigation delivers a few drops where needed instead of flooding the field. An ultra-low-leakage wide-gap access device (off <1e-21 A) lets the capacitor shrink to a planar 0.5 fF, 10x below today's 5 fF pillar, and the bitline is clamped by a virtual-ground charge integrator so the tiny packet lands on a small feedback capacitor without swinging the bitline.
why: Retention stays >1 s with 10x less charge, so charge moved per access falls ~10x and the 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1) and its HAR-etch capital disappear.

title: Refresh cycles double as in-DRAM scrub, zeroing and copy
idea: IFR: refresh does useful work. Each refresh already opens a row into the sense amps, so a small per-bank engine uses that open window to run ECC scrub, bulk zeroing of freed pages and RowClone-style copies queued by the OS, costing no extra activations.
why: Fact 3: turns the 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh into productive work, giving back equivalent channel bandwidth and energy now spent on scrub and zeroing traffic.

title: Compiler-proven tensor lifetimes shorter than retention need zero refresh
idea: Po: data dies before it decays. In AI training, activations and gradients live ~1-10 ms between write and last read; the compiler proves each tensor's lifetime and places it in capacitorless floating-body memory with ~10 ms retention that is never refreshed, while long-lived weights go elsewhere.
why: Facts 1 and 3: lets a cheap, poor-retention capacitorless cell serve 40-60% of training memory with zero refresh energy.

title: Substitute 85 C air-cooled DIMMs with 35 C cold plates
idea: Substitute air cooling with direct liquid cold plates holding DIMMs and HBM at ~35 C, plus a new JEDEC 'cool-tier' mode register that certifies temperature-scaled refresh (leakage halves every ~8-10 C).
why: Running 50 C cooler gives ~16-32x retention; refresh drops at least 8x, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth and the 16-33% idle-power share of refresh.

title: Magnify cells per bit on demand: OS-elastic twin-cell mode
idea: Let the OS/hypervisor flip under-used DRAM regions into 2-cells-per-bit differential mode (complementary cells on paired bitlines) that tolerates ~10x more charge loss and is refreshed at 1 s; regions revert to 1 cell/bit when demand rises, controlled by a per-subarray mode register.
why: Trades idle capacity for refresh: idle rack memory refresh power down ~10x with no process change.

title: Use the dormant knob: PASR plus nightly memory compaction
idea: 10-person constraint: no new silicon, so use what LPDDR already ships. An OS patch compacts movable pages out of whole LPDDR5X segments when load is low, then sets the mode-register partial-array self-refresh (PASR) bits so the empty segments stop refreshing. A watermark policy re-enables them before they are allocated.
why: Fact 3: idle servers and phones often hold 30-60% free memory, and self-refresh energy falls in proportion when it stops being refreshed. It is a kernel patch a small team can upstream.

title: Positive fixed-charge nitride spacer relieves storage-junction GIDL field
idea: Effect: field-effect passivation by fixed dielectric charge (the solar-cell passivation trick). A SiNx spacer holding ~+2e12 cm^-2 fixed charge lines only the gate-to-storage-node overlap, accumulating electrons at the n+ surface so band bending under a low wordline is reduced and GIDL falls. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~10x less GIDL in hold; zero added masks if the spacer deposition is swapped.

title: Eliminate sensing during refresh: node-gated broadcast recharge pulse
idea: Add a small second transistor whose gate is the storage node, linking the node to a shared restore line; a bank-wide pulse on that line tops up every node holding '1' (transistor on) and leaves '0' nodes untouched (transistor off). Refresh becomes one global pulse with no row activation, sense amplifiers or bitline swing.
why: Refresh energy drops from ~46 fJ/bit to a few fJ/bit (no bitline CV^2, no sensing) and refresh no longer blocks banks, recovering 10-20% bandwidth; costs ~30% cell area.

title: Glymphatic sleep-flush pulses empty charge traps in oxide access FETs
idea: The brain flushes waste during sleep; low-temperature gate dielectrics trap electrons under bias, shifting Vt and raising off-current over hours, so right after a row is restored during self-refresh the controller hits its wordline with a short deeper-negative pulse (~-1.5 V, ~100 ns) that detraps them, rotating through all rows.
why: Holds off-current at its fresh value over life, avoiding the 10-100x stress-induced leakage drift of low-temperature oxide FETs, so refresh can be set to fresh-device retention (5-10x longer than aged worst case).

title: Lighthouse-lit rows: photoconductive wide-gap access channels
idea: Random stimulus 'lighthouse': a beam sweeps, and only what it touches is lit. Each row gets a silicon-nitride waveguide carrying a ~365 nm pulse that photogenerates carriers in GaN access channels beneath it; in the dark a 3.4 eV-gap channel has essentially zero intrinsic carriers, so the bit is isolated with no gate voltage at all.
why: Dark current of a wide-gap photoconductor sits orders of magnitude below 1 fA (fact 3) and the 3 V wordline pump disappears (fact 10). Speculative: photocarrier lifetime must be ns-short and waveguide pitch must reach row pitch.

title: Tailor-trimmed access transistors: charge-trap Vt fix for tail cells
idea: Random stimulus 'tailor': alter only the garments that do not fit. Add a thin nitride trap layer to the access gate stack; after retention screening at wafer test, the ~1 ppm leaky cells get a one-time Fowler-Nordheim program pulse that adds ~150 mV of Vt, pulling them back into the main distribution.
why: The refresh interval is set by the worst-ppm tail, not the median; trimming it lets refresh go from 64 to ~512 ms (8x) for all cells (fact 3). Risk: trapped-charge retention over 10 years at 85 C.

title: Per-cell threshold trimming via charge-trap layer in access gate
idea: Po: every access transistor is custom-made. Add a thin SiN charge-trap film inside the buried-wordline gate stack; at wafer test, cells in the leakage tail receive a one-time Fowler-Nordheim program pulse that raises their Vt ~150 mV, tightening the Vt distribution until the tail disappears.
why: Fact 3: a 10x tighter off-current tail lets refresh run 4-8x less often and permits a shallower negative wordline, saving refresh energy and charge-pump area (fact 7).

title: Fill-then-freeze pulses pin telegraph traps in low-leak state
idea: Worse: let variable-retention-time traps flip randomly between high- and low-leak states. Flip: before each idle period apply a calibrated gate/drain pulse that charges the GIDL-enhancing border traps into their neutral configuration, which then persists for seconds because emission time is long.
why: Removes the VRT tail that forces ~2x refresh guard-banding (fact 3).

title: GaN/AlN deep quantum-well storage node with 2 eV barrier
idea: Worse at 125 C: store electrons in a shallow potential well they boil out of. Flip: hold the bit as a 2DEG charge packet in a GaN well clad by AlN barriers (~2 eV offset), written and erased by a gate pulse that lowers the barrier rather than by tunneling through oxide, so endurance is unlimited and thermionic escape is negligible at 125 C.
why: Retention hours to days at 125 C (fact 3), removing almost all refresh.

title: Post-test oxygen-vacancy trimming raises Vt of leakage-tail cells only
idea: O: use an oxide-semiconductor access FET with an oxygen-exchange TaOx gate liner; at wafer test, locate the ~0.01% leakage-tail cells and apply a per-cell high-field gate pulse that pumps oxygen into the channel near the drain, annihilating donor vacancies and permanently raising that cell's Vt ~0.2 V.
why: The tail, not the median, sets refresh (fact 3); trimming the worst 1e-4 of cells could extend the refresh interval 4-10x without touching the rest of the array.

title: KrF excimer melt-anneal recrystallizes storage-node junctions defect-free
idea: Kr: after the storage-node implant, flash the surface with a tens-of-ns 248 nm KrF excimer pulse that melts only the top ~30-50 nm, so the junction regrows by liquid-phase epitaxy, annihilating end-of-range implant loops and forming a box-shaped junction without deep diffusion.
why: End-of-range defects are SRH centers behind junction-leakage tail cells (fact 3); melt regrowth could cut tail leakage ~3-10x using mature non-EUV laser tools.

title: Foundry SONOS as a trim knob: per-cell one-time Vt tuning
idea: 10-person constraint: only foundry-standard options are available to us. Design an eDRAM macro on a mature MPW process that offers SONOS charge-trap transistors, and use the SONOS device itself as the access transistor. At test, measure each cell's leakage and give leaky cells a single program pulse that raises their Vt 0.3-0.5 V for life, deleting the tail cell by cell.
why: Fact 3: the refresh interval is set by the worst cell. Trimming the tail to the median could lengthen refresh ~10x using standard foundry eNVM devices and a test program.

title: Subsea pressure-compensated housings: park standby bitlines at the leaky state's level
idea: Deep-sea electronics survive by equalizing pressure instead of resisting it. During self-refresh, park bitlines at the stored-'1' voltage instead of VDD/2 so '1' cells (which also suffer junction leakage) see zero drain-source voltage and no subthreshold loss, while robust '0' cells' small upward subthreshold leak is partly offset by their own downward junction leak.
why: Targets the weakest state in the tail; could extend worst-case retention 2-4x in idle, where refresh is 16-33% of power (fact 3).

title: Shake out the liars: VRT provocation profiling with thermal and voltage cycling
idea: 10-person constraint: make cheap profiling trustworthy. Before any relaxed-refresh deployment, run a 6-hour provocation routine on the FPGA tester: 25-95 C thermal cycling (chamber or heat gun), VPP/VDD corners and worst-case neighbor data patterns. This makes variable-retention-time cells toggle into their leaky state so they get caught.
why: Fact 3: VRT is the reason profile-based refresh is unsafe. Catching 99%+ of VRT cells makes 4-16x refresh relaxation safe, and the test recipe is something a small lab can sell.

title: Eliminate the substrate body: XeF2-released suspended nanowire gate-all-around access device
idea: Pattern Si nanowires by e-beam lithography, undercut them with XeF2 vapor so they hang free, then wrap them with ALD HfO2/TiN to form a gate-all-around access device with no body contact and no junction to substrate. The storage node connects only to the suspended wire.
why: Removes the junction-to-substrate leakage component and lowers DIBL, cutting off current 10-100x vs recessed-channel devices; all steps are standard university nanofab.

title: Magnify the barrier to vacuum: field-emission-written floating islands
idea: Suspend a metal storage island in a sealed 5 nm vacuum nanocavity, write it by field emission from a sharpened tip electrode (1-2 V across nm gaps), and read it by capacitive coupling to a gain FET. Vacuum has no traps to wear out and essentially no zero-bias conduction.
why: Non-volatile, refresh-free, endurance not limited by oxide damage; uses common metals (Mo, Ti).

title: Vacuum-nanogap field-emission access: electrons cross nothing when off
idea: Inverts 'carriers flow through a solid channel': the storage node ends in a sharp nanotip facing the bitline across a sealed ~10 nm vacuum gap; a wordline gate raises the local field above emission threshold for read/write, while below it the exponential Fowler-Nordheim law gives >10^12 on/off with no channel to leak. Gaps are made by sacrificial-layer release plus a wafer-level hermetic ALD seal.
why: Replaces the leakage tail (fact 3) with an off-current far below aA, enabling refresh-free working memory that is also temperature- and radiation-insensitive.

title: Vacuum-channel field-emission nanotriode as DRAM access device
idea: Po: the transistor channel is empty. Build the access device as a sealed ~10 nm vacuum gap between a sharp emitter tip on the bitline side and the storage node, gated by a wordline ring; electrons cross only when the gate field thins the emission barrier, so the off state has no semiconductor, no junction and no GIDL.
why: Fact 3: eliminates every semiconductor leakage path, enabling refresh intervals of seconds, plus radiation hardness; risk is emission uniformity and tip wear at nanoscale.

title: Venus-lander vacuum nanogap field-emission access switch
idea: Vacuum electronics are the switches that survive Venus' 460 C surface; build each access device as a vertical ~10 nm sealed vacuum gap with a sharp emitter on the storage-node side and a gate ring, so electrons cross by field emission only when the wordline raises the tip field. Off, there is no channel, junction or trap to leak through.
why: Fact 3: junction and subthreshold leakage are gone (only exponentially suppressed Fowler-Nordheim tunneling remains), giving near-static, temperature-immune retention; hermetic nanogap sealing and emitter wear are the risks.

title: Vacuum-nanogap field-emission access device with gated emitter pair
idea: Effect: Fowler-Nordheim field emission into vacuum. A sealed 10 nm vacuum gap sits between the bitline contact and the storage node with sharp emitter tips on both sides (for both write polarities) and a ring wordline gate around the gap; the gate raises tip fields above ~3 V/nm only during access, while at rest a ~4 eV work-function barrier conducts nothing measurable.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): no semiconductor channel means no GIDL, junction or trap-assisted tails; retention bounded by capacitor dielectric; radiation-hard bonus.

title: No carriers in the off-state: vacuum-channel field-emission access device
idea: Limit: the off-state medium must contain no carriers. Build a sealed 20 nm vacuum nanogap between a sharp emitter tip on the storage node and a bitline collector, with a surrounding gate as the wordline. The device turns on only by field emission above a threshold field; below it, Fowler-Nordheim current falls super-exponentially.
why: Fact 3: near-zero off-current makes refresh rare. Field emission is temperature-insensitive, which also removes the hot-temperature doubling of refresh. Speculative because of vacuum sealing and emitter wear.

title: Record-solar-cell passivated contact at the storage-node junction
idea: Record silicon solar cells reach junction saturation currents of ~1-5 fA/cm2 with a ~1.5 nm tunnel oxide capped by doped polysilicon (TOPCon). Form the capacitor-to-access-device contact the same way, so the heavily doped, defective region sits in the poly rather than in the silicon and contact-region generation current collapses.
why: Fact 3: attacks contact-region generation and trap-assisted tunneling, a tail contributor; solar fabs show the process is cheap and high-volume, so it is a low-capital addition.

title: PMIC firmware only: undervolt DRAM rails during self-refresh to measured margin
idea: 10-person constraint: we can design only the DIMM's power path. DDR5 DIMMs carry their own PMIC, so custom PMIC firmware or a custom board steps VDD and VPP down during self-refresh to each module's minimum, found by a boot-time margin sweep, plus a 50 mV guard. Rails return to nominal on exit.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh energy scales roughly as V2, so 10-15% lower rails cut self-refresh energy ~20-28% per DIMM with board and firmware work only.

title: Memory arrays fabricated inside the glass-core package substrate
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge memory with a part every accelerator already needs, the package substrate. Glass-core substrates entering production for large AI packages get panel-processed oxide-TFT 1T1C memory layers in their build-up stack directly under the die shadow, connected by fine-pitch vias, so a slow-refresh capacity tier rides beneath each processor without separate dies or TSVs.
why: Data-movement energy (Fact 5) and the HBM TSV tax (Fact 6) for a capacity tier; panel processing cuts capital per bit; ultralow-leakage TFTs allow ~1 Hz refresh (Fact 3).

title: Magnify isolation: storage node floats on buried oxide, no junction
idea: Form the storage-node contact region on a local buried-oxide pocket created by Si/SiGe selective etch-and-fill, so the storage node touches no p-n junction or substrate and the only leakage paths left are the gated channel and the capacitor.
why: Junction generation and trap-assisted tunneling are a large share of the tail; removing them targets ~10x longer minimum retention.

title: Sandpaper-free planarization by gas-cluster ion beams
idea: Random stimulus 'sandpaper': smoothing without grit. Planarize the array STI fill, wordline cap and landing-pad layers with gas-cluster ion beam (GCIB) location-specific smoothing driven by in-line topography maps, replacing CMP, its slurry and the post-CMP brush/megasonic cleans.
why: CMP plus post-clean is a major UPW and slurry-waste user; dry GCIB on the access module's ~4 planarization steps cuts that water >10x, and damage-free surfaces reduce interface traps (fact 3).

title: Minify bitlines for refresh: 16-cell local sense nodes
idea: Add a hierarchical micro-sense amplifier every 16 cells (placed under the array via bonded CMOS) used only for refresh, so each cell restores against a ~1 fF local bitline rather than a 50-100 fF global one. Normal reads still use the global path.
why: Bitline charge per refreshed bit drops >10x; all subarrays can refresh in parallel, hiding the 10-20% bandwidth loss.

title: Refresh only live sub-row segments using gated local wordlines
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: do only as much as needed. Split each row's local wordline into eight sub-row segments with per-segment 'live' bits set by writes and cleared by OS free/zeroing commands; refresh activates only live segments, so refresh energy and bandwidth scale with resident data rather than capacity.
why: Refresh energy (Fact 3) and overfetch (Fact 8): 2-5x lower refresh energy in partially used memories, far finer than bank-level partial-array self-refresh.

title: Series-stacked access transistors on one pillar exploit stack effect
idea: Worse: trust one transistor to isolate the bit. Flip: stack two gate-all-around segments in series on the same vertical pillar; in the off state the intermediate node floats up and reverse-biases the upper device, cutting subthreshold leakage about 10x at zero footprint cost.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) 10x lower; also helps 3D tiers where a long channel cannot be laid laterally (fact 2).

title: Batik wax-resist: hydrocarbon-inhibited selective deposition self-aligns GIDL offset spacers
idea: Batik artists block dye with wax so color lands only where intended. Use long-chain alkylsilane or alkanethiol inhibitors (no fluorinated SAMs) to block ALD on the gate metal while a SiN/SiOC offset grows only on the junction side, self-aligning a 2-3 nm gate-to-storage-junction underlap that weakens the field driving band-to-band GIDL.
why: Self-aligned underlap without extra lithography cuts GIDL, often the dominant tail mechanism, 3-10x (fact 3) and removes an overlay-limited step (fact 4).

title: Cryosar freeze-out barrier access device for cryogenic memory tiers
idea: Revive IBM's 1959 cryosar, which switched by impact ionization of frozen-out impurities: at 40-77 K, a lightly doped silicon region between storage node and bitline insulates because its dopants are frozen out. A wordline field pulse impact-ionizes the donors so the region conducts for nanoseconds, then it refreezes.
why: Off-state leakage is limited by frozen-out carriers and is effectively zero (fact 3); for memory co-located with cryogenic AI or quantum hardware, refresh disappears and the cell needs no MOS gate stack.

title: Double-barrier resonant tunneling access acts as energy filter
idea: Box: InAs quantum-well storage node x AlSb/InAs/AlSb resonant-tunneling two-terminal access x current sense x 4F2 crossbar x GaSb-on-Si x MBE + bonding. Electrons pass only when wordline-bitline bias aligns the resonant level (target on/off >1e6 within ~0.3 V); off resonance the 2 eV AlSb barriers block, so no transistor is needed.
why: Transistor-free 4F2 cell (~1.5x density) with access at ~0.3-0.5 V (fact 10, CV2 ~4x lower) and leakage set by barrier height (fact 3). Valley current and sneak paths are the risk.

title: Graphene-silicon barristor access with gate-tuned Schottky barrier height
idea: Effect: thermionic emission over a gate-tunable Schottky barrier. The storage node contacts silicon through a graphene electrode whose low density of states lets the wordline shift its work function ~0.5 eV: barrier ~0.9 eV in hold (thermionic current ~aA), ~0.4 eV during access.
why: Leakage and 3D (facts 2, 3, 4): leakage set by barrier height exponentially, not by a 12 nm channel's slope; vertical junction is litho-light and stackable.

title: Let only ones fall: unidirectional-error codes replace frequent refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh must stop every bit from decaying': charge leakage only flips true-cells 1->0 (anti-cells 0->1), so store each row with a Berger-style count code (~10 check bits in opposite-polarity cells) that detects any number of unidirectional errors plus a Z-channel code that corrects them, and stretch refresh until the code margin is nearly consumed.
why: Refresh interval 64 ms -> ~0.5-1 s by tolerating tail-cell decay (fact 3) at ~2-4% storage overhead, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth and refresh energy.

title: Substitute hydrogen-passivated oxide channels with HF-vapor fluorine passivation
idea: Substitute hydrogen, a shallow donor and instability source in oxide semiconductors, with fluorine: oxide-channel access transistors are annealed in anhydrous HF vapor diluted in N2 instead of CF4/Ar plasma. The fluorine fills oxygen vacancies and replaces mobile hydrogen.
why: Fewer subgap states and no hydrogen drift give low, stable off-current (~10x less drift-induced leakage), allowing longer refresh intervals for oxide-channel cells.

title: Flash charge-trap layer for per-cell access-transistor Vt trimming
idea: Add a thin nitride charge-trap film to the access-transistor gate stack (SONOS fused with DRAM). At wafer test, retention-profile every cell, then Fowler-Nordheim program electrons into only the leakiest access devices to raise their Vt by 0.2-0.4 V permanently.
why: Refresh rate is set by the top 0.01-0.1% leakage tail. Trimming those cells lets the whole array refresh at median retention, 64 ms to ~1 s, cutting refresh energy ~90%.

title: Floating-gate shadow block behind each DRAM subarray
idea: A double-poly EEPROM block behind each subarray acts as a nonvolatile shadow (nvSRAM fused with DRAM). Before power-down, rows stream through the sense amps into the shadow and refresh stops; on wake the shadow restores them, and shadowing can be limited to an OS-state slice.
why: Standby refresh energy falls to zero for edge devices that sit idle for hours, and a 1990s EEPROM flow is enough.

title: Direct-tunneling charge-trap cell with second-scale retention
idea: Box: charge in a SiN/HfO2 trap layer x 1.5-2 nm tunnel oxide written by direct tunneling (not Fowler-Nordheim) x gain-transistor sensing x in-array x Si x ALD gate stack. Direct tunneling at ~1.5 V writes in ~10 ns without the high-field damage that limits flash endurance, while trap depth gives seconds of retention.
why: Refresh ~100x rarer (fact 3), no capacitor (fact 1), sub-2 V operation (fact 10); endurance target >1e15 since no hot carriers.

title: Firefly's lantern: photovoltaic row gates driven by waveguide light
idea: A firefly signals with light, not wires. Each electrical wordline becomes a SiN waveguide; per 32-cell segment, a series stack of three nanoscale photodiodes turns a femtojoule light pulse into ~1.5 V of local gate drive, and a shunt pull-down discharges it after the pulse.
why: No long metal wordline is charged from a pump, so gate energy per access falls from pJ to ~fJ optical plus laser wall-plug cost (>=10x), and wordline coupling that drives row hammer disappears.

title: Bit-plane split: mantissa low bits live in relaxed-refresh banks
idea: Scale shift down to the bits inside a number: the controller transposes FP16/BF16 tensors so sign, exponent and top mantissa bits sit in normally refreshed banks while low mantissa bits sit in banks refreshed every 2-4 s, where occasional decay only perturbs the 4th-7th significant bit.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): ~40-50% of weight/activation bits get 30-60x fewer refreshes with <0.1% accuracy impact in tolerant layers.

title: Recirculating CCD loops hold streamed model weights
idea: Buried-channel CCD loops built on 350-180 nm CCD lines hold weights that circulate continuously past a regenerating sense-and-restore stage. Each pass taps the stream out to compute at fixed cadence.
why: Refresh is intrinsic to circulation and there are no row decoders (periphery is 49% of the die, fact 7). The cell is ~4F^2 CCD gates, suiting sequential weight streaming.

title: Crested-barrier capacitor: the capacitor is its own access switch
idea: Inverts 'storage and switch are separate devices': each crossbar node is a floating metal nanolayer between two crested tunnel barriers (e.g., nitride/AlN/nitride trilayers) whose peak collapses at high field, giving ~10^12 current change between the ~3 V write and ~1 V hold; charge on the floating layer is the bit, written in ns by tunneling and read capacitively, from one blanket deposition per deck.
why: No transistor, no capacitor tower, one deposition per deck in 4F2 crossbar stacks, ~100x cheaper per GB; crested barriers reduce oxide stress, aiming at 10^12+ endurance; trade-off: write energy and unproven endurance.

title: Fleet-learned per-row retention atlas built over years
idea: Scale jump from one DIMM to a million-server fleet and time jump from a 64 ms spec to multi-year observation: every server runs low-priority retention probes (write pattern, pause 0.25-4 s, read) in idle banks and uploads per-row results with temperature; a fleet model keyed by die lot, wafer position and age assigns each row a refresh bin loaded at boot, and repeated sightings flag variable-retention cells.
why: Refresh (fact 3): >99.9% of rows retain >1 s, so binning most rows to 256 ms-1 s cuts refresh ops ~4-8x, while fleet statistics catch rare VRT behaviour that a single factory test cannot see.

title: Plasma-panel sustain refresh: threshold-gated global top-up pulses
idea: Revive the AC plasma display's inherent memory, in which a global sustain waveform re-fires only the cells that already hold wall charge: place a sharp threshold element (for example a punch-through diode) between each storage node and a shared sustain plane, then pulse the plane. Only nodes still above threshold (stored 1s) conduct and are topped up to full, while 0s stay below threshold and are left alone.
why: Makes refresh an unaddressed broadcast with no sense amps (facts 3, 8): no row activations, no 128x overfetch, and no row-hammer exposure from refresh (fact 9). Refresh energy could fall 5-10x and its bandwidth cost to ~0.

title: Refresh-interval SKUs: sell DRAM priced by retention bin
idea: Scale jump from wafer sort to market structure: test every die at four refresh intervals (64 ms, 256 ms, 1 s, 4 s at 85 C) and sell long-retention grades at a premium to phones, IoT and cold CXL tiers running relaxed refresh, while short-retention dies go to always-busy AI servers whose traffic refreshes rows anyway.
why: Usable supply and yield (strategy): dies now derated or scrapped for tail retention become sellable, and long-retention bins cut device idle power 15-30%.

title: Delete the electrical wordline: optically gated photoconductive access switch
idea: Limit: no metal wordline is allowed over the array. Each cell's access device is a wide-gap GaN or ZnO photoconductor bridge between the bitline and the storage node. A row is 'opened' by a light pulse through a SiN waveguide with grating taps, fed by edge micro-LEDs or lasers. In the dark the bridge holds almost no carriers.
why: Facts 3, 9 and 10: dark leakage of ~aA nearly eliminates refresh. With no wordlines there is no row-hammer coupling and no 3 V wordline CV2 energy. Risks: photoconductor speed (<1 ns needed) and persistent photoconductivity.

title: Crested-barrier MIM tunnel diode as a two-terminal access device
idea: Revive Mead's 1960 metal-insulator-metal tunnel-emitter work and Likharev's crested-barrier proposal: a nitride/alumina/nitride trilayer with a peaked barrier gives Fowler-Nordheim nonlinearity steep enough that current at half bias is ~1e-9 of full-bias current. It serves as a two-terminal access device between capacitor and bitline, selected by plate-line pulsing, so access devices can stack in BEOL above logic.
why: Removes the silicon access transistor and its leakage tail (fact 3), and enables multi-tier BEOL stacking without lateral transistors (fact 2).

title: Trusted-foundry domestic metals: tungsten-free TiN or poly buried wordlines
idea: Defense trusted foundries prize domestic materials. Replace tungsten in buried wordlines with TiN-only or heavily doped polysilicon; the higher RC makes far-end access devices turn on late and leaves some cells partly restored (~0.5-1% raw BER near row ends), which the code absorbs instead of finer wordline segmentation.
why: Resources: removes a China-~80% tungsten dependency from the array (contacts can move to U.S.-mined molybdenum) at no density cost, with a modest throughput hit at row ends.

title: Porous-silicon sacrificial tiers replace SiGe in 3D DRAM stacks
idea: Scale shift from bulk electrochemistry (porous Si for MEMS and solar) to 3D-DRAM tier formation: grow alternating heavily boron-doped and lightly doped Si epilayers, anodize only the heavy layers into porous Si through slit trenches, then oxidize or etch them away to release lateral access-transistor layers, avoiding scarce Ge and SiGe misfit defects.
why: 3D cell blocker (fact 2): strain-free, defect-free lateral channels shrink the leakage tail and simplify 30+ tier stacks using Si, B and HF chemistry only.

title: SIMOX buried oxide under the storage diffusion
idea: Build cells on 1990s SIMOX SOI so the storage n+ sits directly on buried oxide, shrinking its pn junction to a thin sidewall. A body tie suppresses floating-body bipolar leakage.
why: Junction leakage area falls ~90%, giving a 5-10x longer retention tail for the same cell.

title: Gallium-oxide access transistor exploits self-trapped holes to kill GIDL
idea: Ga: use a beta-Ga2O3 (4.8 eV) channel for the access FET; holes generated by band-to-band tunnelling at the drain edge self-trap as immobile polarons, so they cannot carry GIDL current or charge a floating body, and the n-only material has no hole conduction path.
why: GIDL and floating-body effects drive the leakage tail and amplify row hammer (facts 3, 9); a hole-immobile channel could suppress them ~10^3 while the wide gap lowers thermal leakage further.

title: Self-ordered anodic-alumina pores host lithography-free coaxial access transistors
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: anodise an aluminium foil or Al-coated glass panel so it self-organises into hexagonal nanopores at 30-60 nm pitch (~1e10-1e11 per cm2). ALD lines each pore coaxially with bottom electrode, wide-gap oxide channel, gate dielectric and a wrap gate at the top, with the lower pore volume forming the storage capacitor: gate-all-around access at near-4F2 density without EUV.
why: Attacks capital intensity (Fact 4: 5-7 EUV layers) while GAA electrostatics plus wide-gap channels cut leakage (Fact 3); aluminium is abundant and U.S.-produced. Wordline/bitline addressing at pore pitch is the hard part.

title: Epitaxial silicon stack sets access gate length by thickness, not litho
idea: Si: grow an in-situ-doped n+/p/n+ silicon stack by CVD epitaxy so the vertical channel length (80-120 nm) is fixed by the p-layer thickness to +/-1 nm, then etch DUV-immersion SAQP pillars and wrap a gate-all-around wordline, giving a 4F2 cell at DUV-reachable F of ~18-20 nm.
why: 4F2 instead of 6F2 recovers density without EUV (fact 4), and long, uniform vertical channels shrink the subthreshold leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Retention-binned page allocator matches data lifetime to row strength
idea: Profile each row's retention class at test and store the map in SPD. The OS places frequently rewritten data in weak rows and long-lived data in strong rows, each class refreshed at its own rate.
why: Multi-rate refresh is normally capped by weak rows holding long-lived data. Matching them removes that cap and cuts refresh operations 70-80%.

title: Antiferroelectric ZrO2 gate gives hysteresis-free negative-capacitance access device
idea: Zr: stack a thin antiferroelectric ZrO2 layer on the access-transistor gate dielectric and shift it, via work-function offset, into the negative-slope branch of its double loop, so capacitance matching gives sub-60 mV/dec swing without the memory window of ferroelectric NC-FETs.
why: Steeper slope lets a higher Vt keep on-current, cutting off-leakage ~10x or wordline voltage ~20-30% (facts 3, 10).

title: A patch table on the FPGA: weak bits live in SRAM
idea: 10-person constraint: no die changes. The CXL controller keeps a small CAM/SRAM table (~1 MB per 64 GB) with the address and correct value of every profiled weak bit. Reads are patched on the fly and writes update the table, so the DRAM runs at a refresh interval set by its strong-cell population.
why: Fact 3: the ~0.001% of weak bits stop setting refresh, which can move from 64 ms to over 1 s, at a cost of ~1 MB of SRAM per 64 GB.

title: Judo master's leverage: negative-capacitance HZO gate on access transistor
idea: Judo turns the opponent's force against him. A matched ferroelectric HZO layer in the access transistor's gate stack uses its negative-capacitance region to amplify surface potential, reaching ~35 mV/dec over the critical decades, so the same off-current needs a ~0.5 V lower threshold and the wordline swings ~1.2 V straight from the supply.
why: A pumped 3 V swing becoming a direct 1.2 V swing is ~15x less wordline energy per toggle; HZO serves as a gate amplifier, not as the memory element covered in prior work.

title: Jet-engine power-by-the-hour: vendors sell retained gigabyte-hours
idea: Adapted from Rolls-Royce's power-by-the-hour model: DRAM vendors lease modules and are paid per GB-hour of error-free service, keep ownership, watch retention telemetry remotely, and swap, anneal or re-grade modules before leakage tails cause errors.
why: Gives the maker a profit motive to design repairable, long-lived access devices and to refurbish (fact 3), turning installed DRAM into a reused fleet asset rather than a disposable part.

title: Errors set the refresh rate: ECC-feedback refresh loop
idea: Reverse the control direction: instead of a fixed worst-case tREFI, the controller lengthens each bank's refresh interval stepwise while watching DDR5 on-die ECC error-check-and-scrub counts and its own ECC syndromes, and backs off as soon as corrected errors per row exceed a threshold far below correction capacity. The memory reports its real retention instead of the datasheet predicting it.
why: Most dies retain 4-10x longer than spec at real temperatures, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~50-75% (fact 3); firmware on existing DDR5.

title: Camel HBM rated to 125 C enables waterless warm cooling
idea: Random stimulus 'camel': built to tolerate heat instead of drinking to stay cool. Rate a hot SKU of HBM to 125 C junction by combining an elevated-Vt array (+150 mV gate work function), base-die refresh that scales with temperature and hot-screened dies, so accelerator coolant loops can run 45-50 C inlet and reject heat through dry coolers all year with no evaporation.
why: HBM's ~85-95 C ceiling often forces cold coolant and evaporative towers; dry cooling takes memory-attributable cooling water from ~1.5-2 L/kWh to near zero, far more than 10x, with the extra leakage at temperature (fact 3) absorbed by design.

title: Wine-cellar retention bins sell short-retention dies to rewrite-heavy buyers
idea: Random stimulus 'wine cellar': each vintage goes to the buyer it suits. Bin dies by measured retention: long-retention bins (>=1 s) sell at a premium to edge/mobile, while dies failing the 64 ms spec, now scrapped or repaired, ship to AI training racks with a 16 ms controller-managed refresh, where data is rewritten every few ms anyway.
why: Converts retention-yield loss into supply; recovering a few percent of dies at today's 4x prices adds real bits and dollars (cost per bit, usable supply).

title: Convert U.S. silicon-carbide power fabs into refresh-free SiC DRAM lines
idea: C (as SiC): retool 150/200 mm 4H-SiC power-device fabs in NC, NY and TX with existing DUV steppers to build SiC MOS 1T1C cells, whose 3.26 eV gap gave early research SiC DRAM cells orders-of-magnitude longer room-temperature retention than silicon, and sell them as a big-cell, refresh-free working-memory tier behind DRAM on CXL.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturable memory supply (U.S. ~1-2% share) with tools already installed and no EUV (fact 4), and removes refresh (fact 3); lower density means it wins on capital per usable GB, not on die density.

title: Hibernating-bear wordlines hold their own negative bias, pumps off
idea: Random stimulus 'hibernating bear': store reserves, then shut the metabolism down. On entering deep idle, each wordline is charged to -1 V and its driver disconnects, so the wordline's own capacitance holds the negative bias like a DRAM cell with a slow top-up every few seconds; negative pumps and bias generators power down while access leakage falls ~1000x.
why: Idle memory energy (refresh plus pumps, 16-33% of idle power, fact 3) falls ~10x, and the water embedded in that electricity (generation plus cooling, ~2 L/kWh) falls by the same 10x.

title: Substitute excimer and EUV lithography with nanoimprint for wordline trenches
idea: Substitute ArF scanners (argon/neon gas laser) and EUV (CO2 drive laser with helium in its gas mix) with UV-LED-cured nanoimprint from e-beam-written masters for the buried-wordline and active layers. The periodic DRAM array suits imprint, which reproduces the master's ~1 nm line-edge roughness.
why: Lower line-edge roughness gives tighter access-transistor Vt and leakage spread (sigma-Vt down ~30%), shrinking the tail that sets refresh, while cutting litho capex and rare-gas use.

title: IBM X-ray proximity lithography revived for uniform access pillars
idea: Revive IBM's 1990s X-ray lithography program in Vermont with a U.S.-built compact inverse-Compton light source: ~1 nm X-rays expose access-transistor pillars with near-vertical, highly uniform sidewalls and negligible diffraction-driven CD variation, replacing EUV for the critical access layers.
why: Pillar CD variation drives Vt variation and the leakage tail (fact 3); ~2x tighter CD sigma shortens the tail, and the single-supplier EUV dependence goes away (fact 4).

title: E-ink microcapsule bit: charged nanoparticle parked top or bottom
idea: Scale e-paper microcapsule manufacturing to a sealed ~10 nm cage holding one charged nanoparticle or ion cluster, held by image-charge adhesion to the top or bottom electrode. It is moved by a field pulse and read by capacitance difference.
why: Zero refresh: position is held by adhesion with no leaking charge and no hold power. The ns transit over 10 nm in vacuum is the speculative part.

title: Decay-tracking reference voltage widens aged-cell sense margin
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA whose reference comes from a replica cell pair written at the last refresh and leaking in parallel x in-mat x Si x design only. Because true-cell 1s decay while 0s stay, the reference drifts down with the average 1, keeping the decision point midway between a decayed 1 and a 0.
why: Usable signal for aged cells roughly doubles, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh interval (fact 3) with no process change.

title: Magnify restore voltage only on refresh: overdrive write-back
idea: During refresh (not normal access) sense amps restore '1' cells to ~1.4 V from a separate boosted restore rail with a brief overdriven wordline, storing ~40% more charge so cells take longer to decay to the sense threshold; normal accesses keep the low VARY.
why: Retention ~1.5-2x longer so refresh frequency halves; net refresh energy ~30-40% lower; dielectric reliability is the watch item.

title: Substitute explicit refresh with weight-streaming reads that restore rows
idea: Substitute refresh commands for LLM weight regions with read-restore. During decode every weight row is activated once per token (~20-50 ms), and each activation fully restores its charge, so the controller tracks how often each row is read and suppresses refresh while serving. This is controller logic only, with no fab step.
why: Weights fill most HBM capacity in inference, so refresh there is pure waste: ~10% of bandwidth and refresh energy recovered.

title: Eliminate explicit refresh for weights re-read every inference pass
idea: The controller keeps a per-row touched-this-window bit; in LLM serving, where weight rows are streamed every token (<20-50 ms), rows proven read within tREFW get REF suppressed because each activation already restores the cells. A watchdog issues REF only to rows the access pattern missed.
why: Weight-streaming inference touches most of HBM per token; suppressing redundant refresh recovers ~10-20% bandwidth and ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy across the weight footprint.

title: LLM decode sweeps counted as refresh: implicit-refresh accounting
idea: In AI inference each decode token reads the whole live KV cache every ~20-60 ms, and every activation restores its row. A per-row last-activated timestamp in the controller marks rows a sweep recently touched and drops them from the refresh schedule, so only cold rows get explicit refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 8: for KV-cache-dominated HBM most explicit refresh disappears, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth refresh takes at 32-64 Gb, with no device change.

title: Pressed-flower 2 nm silicon channel widens the bandgap
idea: Random stimulus 'pressed flower': flatten it and its properties change. Thin the vertical access channel to a 2-3 nm sheet by self-limited oxidation and strip, where quantum confinement raises silicon's effective bandgap by ~0.2-0.3 eV and gives near-ideal gate control.
why: A wider effective gap suppresses band-to-band GIDL and generation current exponentially, and swing approaches 60 mV/dec: tail leakage down ~10x (fact 3). Risk: mobility and on-current loss, sheet-thickness variation.

title: Abacus-bead Coulomb-blockade island isolating the storage node
idea: Random stimulus 'abacus bead': beads move one at a time and only when pushed. Place a sub-2 nm silicon nanodot between the access channel and the storage node; its >0.3 eV charging energy blocks single-electron leakage when the wordline is off, and the wordline lowers the blockade to let charge through.
why: Coulomb blockade gives a non-thermionic off state that does not share the subthreshold tail (fact 3). Speculative: room-temperature blockade needs atomically controlled dot size and must still pass ~1e4 electrons per access.

title: Cactus clean: anhydrous in-situ surface prep for access gates
idea: Random stimulus 'cactus': it thrives on almost no water. Replace the HF-last/SC1/SC2 wet sequences before the access-transistor gate oxide, buried-wordline liner and storage-contact epi with a cluster-tool chain of anhydrous HF/NH3 vapor etch, atomic-hydrogen radical clean and in-situ ALD, with no air break, so no native oxide ever needs a wet strip.
why: The access-device module carries ~20 pre-clean steps at ~20-50 L of UPW per wafer each; dry in-situ prep cuts that module's water >10x and lowers interface-trap density, which also trims the leakage tail (fact 3).

title: Snowball CO2 aerosol and supercritical rinse for wordline trenches
idea: Random stimulus 'snowball': a frozen projectile cleans, then disappears. Post-etch particle removal in high-AR buried-wordline trenches and vertical-channel pillars uses cryogenic CO2 snow jets followed by a supercritical-CO2 rinse/dry with a little cosolvent, replacing DI megasonic rinses and IPA drying; the CO2 is recaptured and recycled.
why: Removes DI-rinse and IPA-dry water from the access module (>10x less on those steps) and eliminates capillary collapse of 60:1 structures, a yield loss that falls on leakage-critical pillars.
